utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, are you ready to continue with Mr. Jakupovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. Just before I call him in, your Honours, I have a copy of the letter that we sent to the International Police Task Force, and their reply in relation to the use of the facilities in Banja Luka and our attempt to interview the Defence witnesses there which was raised in the motion that was discussed earlier. I have a copy for your Honours and I will hand that to you. The letter and its reply are self-explanatory.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am so anxious I do not know that I want to wait to read the letter. What do they say, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. I do not need to read the letter then. Of course, I will read the letter. Do you have anything to report, either Mr. Kay or Mr. Orie, on this situation, not the letter so much? The Chamber had decided that at the request of the Defence we would have a recess at the conclusion of the Prosecutor's case in chief. The estimate of the Prosecutor when we last spoke was that they would finish August 14th but that, of course, does not include any time for cross-examination. My guess would be probably the last week of August maybe we will conclude, but you, lawyers, know better than I.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then we had decided, the parties had decided, that that time would be used for the Prosecutor to interview alibi witnesses and the Defence would be present. Mr. Niemann had suggested that that period in September might cause some problems because the election is 18th. He had heard there might be some difficulties in terms of just access to people and the conditions that might or might not exist there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you have any information?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I can probably assist the Court. I have been talking to the Prosecution during this week over the timing for the conclusion of the case. We are all of the view that it should end Friday week.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That would be ----

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think it is 16th.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is Friday, 16th. There may be a trickle over into the following Tuesday and we have made arrangements on our side that we will be leaving here on Saturday, two of us from the Defence team, to go to Banja Luka. Mr. Wladimiroff will be going over slightly later just to deal with the eventuality if the case does go over into that week after 16th, and he can handle any witnesses that are to be dealt with. We are making our arrangements so that Ms. De Bertodano and myself are there for a week to do a final review and round up of witnesses and advising them of the procedures as well as continuing our investigations. We still have about 10 or 12 more witnesses who need interviewing over there and documents to get hold of. Mr. Wladimiroff's stay will overlap ours, so that he is there for a few days longer to deal with any further eventualities. On a practical level, it really does seem that a break between the two cases is highly desirable. I know the Prosecution would probably welcome it in relation to their investigations, but to enable the Defence case to function at all as we have no control over our witnesses, them not being close to hand. If the Court was receptive to a three-week break that may even be more helpful, to start somewhere around about 10th September.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That was just what I was going to ask you, just how much time then were you thinking about? You have no information on the feasibility of your interviewing witnesses at that time?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We are going to attempt it the week after the trial, and we will see what we can do. We will, of course, keep the Court informed of all developments.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Judge Stephen reminds me that we will be meeting with the Deputy Registrar this Thursday, tomorrow, they have returned, and I have spoken in passing really, but we will have more information at least regarding their efforts on a number of matters. Does the Defence plan on submitting a motion to dismiss as to any of the counts at the close of the Prosecutor's case in chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There may well be. We have talked about this and we thought that the opportunity would be to submit a motion between a break in the cases, so that the Court was able also to consider the matter prior to the Defence case starting, and that would help perhaps narrow the issues that have to be tried.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Or just eliminate all of the issues if you are very successful, you know!

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: One is ever hopeful.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I did want to know whether that was your plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That would be helpful if we heard argument then on that before the recess, that is what you are saying, then of course we would consider whatever your submissions were during the recess and the Prosecutor's response.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. I do not see us being able to achieve such a brief before the recess, because of the volume of work that is required. It is really all hands to the pumps, as far as we are concerned, in presenting the case at the moment as well as concentrating on the Defence side.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK, so then you would be submitting a written brief and the Prosecutor would respond. You are suggesting we consider that during the recess?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK, very good. Yes, Mr. Niemann, you are ready to proceed with Mr. Jakupovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good, thank you. MR. ADIL JAKUPOVIC, recalled Examined by MR. NIEMANN, continued.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You will not submit a written brief before the recess. You will submit it at some point so we can consider it during the recess though?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So that we will be able to consider it before we resume the case again in September?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is what we had aimed to do. We are delegating tasks at the moment amongst the team.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. Thank you. Mr. Jakupovic, you are still under oath, do you understand that, the oath that you took yesterday to tell the truth? You are still under that oath. Do you understand that, Mr. Jakupovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Jakupovic, at the conclusion of the hearing yesterday afternoon you were telling the Chamber about a meeting that you had had with Mr. Tadic and a gentleman who said that he came from Velika Kladusa concerning your house in Kozarac. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During the course of this conversation did anyone suggest to you that you should leave the camp and go away with them to some place in order to sign up relating to this transfer of the house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, before that it was not a sale, it was an exchange, you see.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not to sell but to exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No. Was there any suggestion that this should have been put formally into some sort of writing or that there should be some document that you should sign and that you should go away and do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who suggested that to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was suggested both by Tadic and the other one to go and put down the contract on paper because he could not go to his place and I could not go to mine, so that we should have papers, this man said, so that I would not be given a barn instead of a real house, it would be good to do it, which I refused because I could not and I said that, whoever other people were. Had I been ordered to do that, I would have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Why did you refuse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was war. One could be killed any moment and I guess it was the desire for life, fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So you were afraid to leave the camp, was that the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure, I did not leave it even for a millimetre.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened then when you said you would not go with them to sign the paper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing. The two of them left and I went to the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you tell me how Dusko Tadic was dressed on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the predominant colour in the camouflage uniform that he had on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Why, camouflage uniform with a blue foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you recall whether he had any arms in his possession at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe they had, that both of them had automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did Mr. Tadic have a hat or any form of head wear at the time that you can recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Believe me, I do not remember whether he had a cap ----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you recall whether ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: --- or perhaps in his hands or at the belt, I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say the "belt", do you mean the hat may have been tucked in the belt?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, either tucked in the belt or in his hands or on the head, I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you recall whether Mr. Tadic had a beard on this occasion or was he clean shaven?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did not have a beard, but he was not quite clean shaven. It could have been a day's growth perhaps, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did he have any insignia or markings on the clothing to indicate to whom he was attached, to what organisation he was attached?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On his sleeve he had "police", that is, milicija in Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The other gentleman that was with Mr. Tadic that spoke to you and who said he had come from Velika Kladusa, how was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He also had a camouflage uniform on, but I believe it was an army one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to show you some photographs, if I may? First of all, could you just look at this photograph that I show you and I would like it to be marked for identification No. 301? Would you just look for me for the moment, please, Mr. Jakupovic, at the photograph that I am now showing you and can you tell me whether you recognise the building that is shown in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do know this building very well. This is the primary school at Trnopolje, and the building of the co-operative on the other side, as a matter of fact, the cinema hall with the gymnasium.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I would ask if that photograph could be put on the overhead projector? Mr. Jakupovic, I am going to ask you again with the pointer to point to the various buildings that you have just described. Thank you. Can you just describe the buildings in that photograph again, please, pointing to them with the pointer? When you point with the pointer, just leave the pointer on the building long enough so that we can see it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [The witness indicated on the photograph]. This is the north part of the school. This is the entrance into the gymnasium. This is the hall and this is the co-operative, where the co-operative premises were, and the hall and this is the chimney of the boiler room.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. I tender that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 301 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you now look at the next photograph that I show you? Might it be marked 302? That is photograph 40/13 for the Defence. [To the witness]: Do you recognise the photograph that you have now been shown, Mr. Jakupovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This building is a building materials store which was within the confines of the Trnopolje camp and the transformer substation also was there across the school and the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might that be placed upon the screen, please? Just with the pointer again, Mr. Jakupovic, very slowly would you point to the area which the camp was contained in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [The witness indicated on the photograph]. The area, this part from above, comes the road from Kozarac to the railway station. This part goes to Prijedor and this is the transformer substation. This again belonged to the co-operative before, it was the shop selling building materials, and in the background you can see the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you recall whether at any stage when you were at the camp there were any guard posts or checkpoints in this vicinity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I could see, I mean, entering from Prijedor, I think that this, next to this house was one of the checkpoints. Another one was somewhere here on this road towards the railway station. There is a junction immediately behind it. There was one and then one in the direction of Kozarac ----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You need to go much slower ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: --- and that is where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: --- otherwise we do not follow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of the points was here on the Prijedor road, around this house ----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Just stop for a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: --- towards Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The next one? Perhaps you would point to the next one and just stop leaving the pointer there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [The witness indicated on the photograph]. The second one was here or perhaps a little bit further away because there are two more roads here, one leading to the railway station and the next one runs in parallel with the railway tracks, so there was one of the points.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Stopping there. The next one that you pointed to, could you put the pointer there and leave your pointer at that spot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [The witness indicated on the photograph]. The next one was on the road leading to Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I tender that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 302 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might you look at the next photograph that I show you, 303, and might that be marked for identification 303? Mr. Jakupovic, do you recognise that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know, that is the old co-operative building with the cinema theatre in Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might that be placed upon the screen, please? Just looking at that photograph, Mr. Jakupovic, were prisoners kept in any part of this building from what you remember of the time when you were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The cinema theatre, this part, that was full.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. I tender that photograph, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 303 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I would ask you, please, to have a look at the next photograph. Might it be marked 304? Just looking at that photograph, Mr. Jakupovic, do you recognise the building that is shown in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This could be the northern side of the school in Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you uncertain about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is no fence here, now that was there -- oh, I am sorry, there is, yes, yes, there is a fence. That is the northern part of the school of Trnopolje. There is a very small fence ----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: OK.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: --- of wire fence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Could you put that, please, on the screen? I tender that photograph, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 304 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might the map that I have just handed to the usher please be marked for identification 305? Mr. Jakupovic, I would ask you to look at the map that you have now been shown. Would you please familiarise yourself with it and tell me if you recognise the markings on the map, if you recognise that map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might the map be placed upon the screen, please? Mr. Jakupovic, I am going to ask you to point to the various localities on that map, but when I ask you to do it, would you please put the pointer there and leave it for the time being so everyone can have a good look at it? Firstly, could you point to the location of where the school was at Trnopolje, as part of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The school was here, this part.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is where the initials "SK" are, is that right, "SK"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "SK", yes, but that is a complex. There is a new school. There is a co-operative building. There is a store, the buildings supplies store.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are they all on the left-hand side of the yellow road as you look at the plan, as you look at it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, when you go from the railroad station to the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I will ask you to point, please, to the railway station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The railroad station here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is towards the bottom of the map immediately above the "C" in the word "Kozarac". Can you point to the fish farm, please, where the fish farm was located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The fish farm and it continues down, about nine to 10 kilometres by three kilometres about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the name of the fish farm, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sanicani.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you point, please, to the road that goes to Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the railway station, the road up to Kozarac, six kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you point to the road that goes to Prijedor, the old road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this part there is this old road, that is the old road, and the new one is up there, north.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you point to the road that goes to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It goes along the tracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. For the sake of the transcript, your Honour, might it be noted that the witness pointed to the yellow road leading from the bottom centre of the map to the top of the map, the road to Prijedor being the road from the bottom centre of the map to the top left-hand side of the map, and the road to Omarska being the road from the bottom centre of the map to the right-hand bottom corner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, I suppose there is no explicable reason why Trnopolje never appears by name on any of these maps?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I do not know the answer to that, but I will ask the witness. He may know, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: No, he will not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I do not know, your Honour. I might indicate, your Honour, that written right across the map starting from the top left-hand corner down is the word "Trnopolje", but whether that means the region, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is an area with multiple villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. I tender that map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 305 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Jakupovic, when you were living in Kozarac, during the time that you lived there, did you make application, apply for and obtain a driving licence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Driver's licence I got in 1970. I took the course and I did, that was in 1970, I do not know exactly the month. It was summer, June or July, when I passed the test.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Up until when, approximately, did you keep that driving licence valid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember exactly whether I was extending it or not, but I know that it had expired a long time ago, and I was building a house and I decided not to ever get a car -- I had my reasons -- so that I did not extend it. I do not know what you are interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you please look at this which I now show you? Perhaps it might be marked for identification 306? Perhaps the licence could be marked 306A and the document that is with it marked 306B? Your Honours, I am a bit concerned, I am not sure that if the sticker is placed on the document it may damage the document. So if it, perhaps, could be placed on the accompanying document, that may be better? Perhaps the witness could be shown just 306A, not B, 306A? Mr. Jakupovic, would you look at the document that I have now shown you, 306A, and can you tell me, do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is my driving licence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Does this driving licence contain the date of its expiration, the date that it expired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it says 12.6.85.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, so 12th June 1985?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I tender the licence, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: What is the possible relevance of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This licence was found in the premises of Mr. Tadic ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: --- in Germany. I tender the licence, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 306A will be admitted. B has not been identified yet, has it, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, that is the document from the German police, if it could be marked for identification, I will tender it at some subsequent stage. Mr. Jakupovic, the licence that you have just seen, your licence, when did you last see this document, apart from now and when it was shown to you by both the German police and by myself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe after, or maybe a year or two after its expiration date. I was planning on extending it, but when I realised that there was a medical test and other tests, then I decided that I am not going to extend it or buy the car or anything. So I just kept it like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know where you kept it, Mr. Jakupovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had two boxes, one tin one, and there was all my documentation. In which one of the two it was, I rarely was looking. My wife usually kept it and ordered it there. It was in one of those two boxes with the passports and other documents, receipts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: These documents were in your house in Kozarac, were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In what part of the house did you keep these documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In a room, upstairs there was a room, and I had an armoire there. I do not know how to explain it, which part. It was in one of these armoires.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: "One of these armoires", what is an armoire? Can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is like a cupboard, it has doors.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you left Kozarac, did you take these documents with you or did you leave them in the house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From all the family, it was only I who had licna karta, and it is for a reason I once paid a fine for not having it so I always kept it on me, and the rest, they never did. I do not blame my wife or my children, I thought that it would all come -- and also we, in fear, we did not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So are you saying you left it behind when you left Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, everything stayed there, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Jakupovic, did you at any stage say to Mr. Tadic that he could have possession of your licence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I never told him and he never asked me. It is a useless document. It was only for me, maybe I could brag at some point that I had passed the test, but it had no value.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Jakupovic, do you know a man by the name of Bosko Dragicevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do know him. He was my colleague from work.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know what nationality or ethnic group he was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, his father was a Serb and the mother was Croat, so a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know where they lived or do you know where he lived, I should say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know. He lived next to his father's house. There is a triangle where roads cross on the road Kozarac, the old road that goes to Banja Luka/Prijedor, so where that triangle is to the right, in Kozarac itself, so to speak, in the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Exhibit [redacted]?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you mean a plaque showing the city of Kozarac with Marsala Tita going down the street?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, I understood [redacted] to be a photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Bos has told me that this Exhibit is confidential or, at least, it was offered through a witness who had received certain protective measures. You may handle it, I suppose, as you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It depends upon what you ask this witness, I suppose, regarding this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. I have another copy of it. I suppose I could use that but it is the same photograph, so .....

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If there is no objection to using this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No. The questions I ask will not .....

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you recognise that photograph, Mr. Jakupovic, the area that is depicted in it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you see in the photograph the area where the house of Bosko Dragicevic is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Where it is situated?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, could that photograph be placed on the screen? Could you point to that part of the photograph where the house of Mr. Bosko Dragicevic is located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This roof is Bosko Dragicevic's roof, this roof. This is the house of his father and this is the store, this is, and behind that is his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Jakupovic, would you now please look around the courtroom and tell me if you can see the person that you know and recognise as Dule Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you please point to him and would you describe the clothing that he has on and where he is located in the court room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is between the two policemen in the navy blue suit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. Might the record reflect, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, the record will reflect that the witness identified the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Jakupovic, before the attack on Kozarac, is it right that most of the Serbs had left that town in the days and weeks before the shelling started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, 100 per cent I cannot tell, but on the last day there was nobody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Some Muslim families as well had left the town in the days and weeks before that shelling started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To be honest, I do not know. There were those who were that smart.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you remember the Tadic family leaving about three weeks before the shelling started at the beginning of May with the priest, Mladen Majkic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But the Tadic family had left their home some weeks before the shelling started, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you remember Dusko being there at the family home on his own for some time and then him leaving?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was with Dusko before the shelling, maybe two days. I do not know if it is 100 per cent two days, maybe three, but I did not ask him where his family was and he did not tell me, so I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: During the attack on Kozarac and when you left the town you did not see Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: As you have told us, you saw him in Prijedor and you mentioned ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: --- two occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: One occasion you told us about when you went to the police station with him and ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: --- what he was doing there was giving a guarantee as to your character?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Because you were concerned to leave the area as you appreciated that it was dangerous for a Muslim living in Prijedor or being anywhere in that district, is that not right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is right, and there was -- I had nothing to live from, I did not have anything to eat. There was nothing positive there so that I would decide to stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. You had been given help that meant you and your family were not put in the camps but were living in Prijedor because you knew this man or had some connection with Zoran Karlica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know that they had any connection, the two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Because it seemed, from what you have told us, that when you left Kozarac and you were at the Limenka bus station that a soldier came and said, "You know Zoran Karlica" and that was why you were taken to Prijedor, is that how it happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please repeat it one more time? I did not get it quite.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It seemed, from what you have told us, that when you left Kozarac soon after the shelling had stopped that you went to the Limenka bus station and you were approached by a soldier who said, "You know Zoran Karlica", and that was why you went to Prijedor rather than going into a camp, is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is, it was, I got down from the Mount Kozara with several thousand people -- there were more arriving -- and I was standing with my family and my neighbour and his mother, all together, for a while, I do not know how long. Then at one point a soldier arrived and whether I was Adil Jakupovic, I said, "Yes". He says, "Come with me, Zoran Karlica is calling you", and we went there behind and there he was indeed. He put us in some military vehicle. He asked us where he could take us, and my neighbour said that he had his wife's mother in Prijedor, and so he took us there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It was in Prijedor where you stayed for some months before eventually moving to Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I spent four months in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Having left Kozarac after the attack on it, is it right that you never returned back to your home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Never more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What happened to your things, your possessions and your home, you have never been able to see for yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I could never learn.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The point of you going to the Prijedor police station with your various guarantees that you had paid your bills, that you were of good character, was again a way of you trying to get a certificate to enable you to leave the area, was that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Why, yes, they were not guarantees. They were simply the receipts that you had paid all sorts of things, and then also the certificate that I was leaving my place of residence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So it seemed that Dusko Tadic in going to the police station with you on that day was helping you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because I would not have dared go there to get this paper because if a male was found in the queue, it was quite possible that he would be taken out of that queue that same moment and that was going to the point of no return.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you went to the SUP on this occasion, you went with Dusko Tadic because he was a policeman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but at that moment he was not wearing the police uniform. He was in civilian, but I suppose he simply had his time off at the time. He was in the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, you knew he was working as a policeman at that time you were in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, my brother-in-law had told me so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You referred to two occasions meeting him in Prijedor. We have heard of this one occasion. Can you remember what the second occasion concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And the second time was in Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Trnopolje for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two months to a day, from 2nd October to 2nd December.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In that time when you were there, do you know who was the Camp Commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was an educator. Before the war he was a school principal, otherwise his name was Slobodan Kuruzovic, a reserve Major, I believe he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you remember who his Deputy Commander was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you have any more dealings with Dusko Tadic after that occasion you met him in Trnopolje and there was the discussion about the transfer of your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any redirect, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to Mr. Jakupovic being permanently excused?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Jakupovic, you are permanently excused. You are free to leave. Thank you for coming. You may leave now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I thank you too. I should like especially to thank you and those who appointed you. This is the only hope of life, the only reason to go on living for me and my people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I call Nasiha Jakupovic. NASIHA JAKUPOVIC, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Does the usher know to bring in the next witness or who the next witness is? Did you offer B -- I forget the number on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If the Defence have no objection, I will offer it, your Honour, otherwise formally I would have tendered it through an investigator to give evidence of how he came into possession of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No objection. We know the source of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. Prosecution Exhibit 306B then will be admitted. Mrs. Jakupovic, would you take the oath, please, that is being given to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mrs. Jakupovic, would you state your full name, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nasiha Jakupovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 8th August '46, Besici near Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Besici is a little village close to Kozarac, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you attend primary and secondary school in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you live there for most of your life, firstly, with your family and then subsequently with your husband?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was an infant when my brother brought me to Kozarac from Besici. We had a flat and then my father built a house and we lived in Kozarac all our lives until the war in the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think the transcript says "brother", but I think you mean "mother" brought you to Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Father", I do not understand, excuse me. I do not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who brought you to Kozarac? Did you come to Kozarac with your parents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With my father and my mum.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. In the latter part leading up to just prior to the war, did you live with your husband in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on Marsala Tita Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your husband is Adil Jakupovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you in Kozarac when the town of Kozarac was shelled in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was at home with my children and my husband, and then we went next house but one to a kind of a basement cellar under the house with other neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you then move from that place out of the centre of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we went towards the forest, towards Debeli Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Sometime after you had been in the forest, did you then meet up with your husband after some days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure, with my husband and my elder son.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After some further days, did you then go with your husband and the rest of your family down from the forest back into the town of Kozarac itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you arrived in Kozarac were you, your husband and your family then taken from there to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who was it that assisted you in going to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we arrived at the intersection Prijedor/Banja Luka next to the petrol station, we got off the car because our neighbour had a car and that was what we rode to that point. At that moment, a military vehicle, a Pitzgauer, came. Zoran Karlica arrived, a good friend of my husband's, a mountaineer, and he looked at us from the car, stopped it, and my neighbour, Sead Kusuran, and myself with the whole family, with my husband, sons and daughter, and took to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you then move into a house in Prijedor where you stayed for a period of some two months?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, to a building not far from the hospital in Prijedor called Urije.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you then move to another building in Prijedor where you stayed for a further two months?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, since we were 15 there, we had nothing to eat, we moved to Raskovac in Prijedor -- only my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Then after that did you then move to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that? Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After that did you then move to the camp at Trnopolje with your family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as we still did not have anything to eat, we went there so that we could get some food through the Red Cross, me and my husband and three children.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know the accused Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know his family, his wife and children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I also know his family, the first, his first child, daughter Valentina, to his father, Ostoja, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you friendly with Dusko Tadic's wife?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure. We were neighbours. We would greet one another every time and we exchanged visits.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you from time to time go to the Tadics' house and did they from time to time come up to your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When I say "they", was that both Dusko Tadic and his wife, Mira?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mira.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were living in Prijedor during the period of the war, did you from time to time have to go out and buy supplies and shopping?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand that question. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In fact, I have just noticed something on the transcript that I would like to correct anyway. I just want to go back and ask you a question again. When you say "they" visited your house, was it both Mr. Tadic, Dusko Tadic, and his wife, Mira?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The next question I asked you was when you were living in Prijedor, during the period of the war, after the attack on Kozarac, did you have to go out and buy food and supplies from time to time in the marketplace?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, since my husband could not leave the house, being a male, and my sons also could not come out, my husband did not leave the house for six months, so I was the only one who had to supply, to obtain supplies for the family.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On one occasion when you were out obtaining these supplies, did you meet with Mira Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you remember when that was, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It happened when we arrived to that other house after -- a month after the arrival.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So, that was about three months after the attack on Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you tell us the circumstances of how it is that you came to meet her and see her?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, she recognised me and I her, of course, logically, since we spent our lives in Kozarac, "What is new? Your kids?" and things like that. Then I asked her, "Please, could you, your husband or you alone bring us our personal papers, documents, from our house".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you asked her this question, what did she say to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She said, "Nasiha, no problem in a day or two I will go with my husband to Kozarac and I shall do my best to get for them you".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you explain to her the documents in particular that you wanted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I explained that I was looking for a school certificate for my two sons, three passports that were in the house of my elder sons, mine and my husband's, because my other son was under age and did not have a passport of his own, and my own ID card.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you tell her where these documents were located in the house in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, well, as they used to come to us too, we would have a cup of coffee or birthday parties and things, he knew the rooms in my house. I explained that it was in the room with the door to the balcony. On the shelf in the third drawer there was a plastic bag and that plastic bag contained all the personal documents of our family.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was there any discussion between the two of you as to when you would meet again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, she told me, "I will be going in a day or two when my husband is free, we shall go to Kozarac, look for it and bring you them".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the next thing that happened in relation to this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then we met again at the same marketplace, because that is where they sold vegetables and other food supplies and other household supplies, and I met her and she said, "Nasiha, do come, I have brought some things for you from your house", and I went with my daughter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did she tell you where she lived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, she pointed the building she was living in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you then go to that house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I went back home, left the purchases and went with my daughter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I said "house" but was it an apartment building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A flat, yes. It was a residential block. A block of apartment buildings there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you went to the house who was there when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was Dusko Tadic's mother, there was Mira, two daughters, Dusko's, and then I arrived with my daughter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was Dusko Tadic there when you first arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He arrived after some 10 or 15 minutes to that flat in which we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you first arrived, did you ask Dusko Tadic's wife about the things that you had asked her to get from the house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I asked her and he himself said, "Here it is, what we found, but since everything is scattered around in your house I will try to search for more".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did they give you? When they said, "Here it is", what did they hand to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They handed me over a doll for my daughter, then an old photo album and a piece of handy work round in shape like this. That was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you receive any of the identification documents such as passports and so forth that you requested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did either Mira or Dusko Tadic say anything to you about those documents that in particular you were interested, the identification documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They said that things were all thrown about around the house and they failed to find them. That was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On this occasion how was Dusko Tadic dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dusko Tadic was dressed in a camouflage uniform, then with a white belt and he had a pistol. I know nothing about calibres but he did not pull it out. It was in the holster and he had a knife. I do not know on which side of his body, but somewhere near the pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the predominant colour of the camouflage uniform that he had on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, sort of blue, I think. I do not know much about that. I believe it was something blue. It was multi-coloured, but I think there was blue in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Apart from the pistol that you spoke of, did he have any other arms on his possession that you could see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw a knife but I would not know what its length would be, not to a centimetre.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see whether or not he had any head wear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As he was getting ready he said, "Sorry, I have got to go on duty because I shall be on duty at Tukovi", and he had in front a pouch also on his belt and he had his cap also tucked behind the belt, but I could not see what kind of a cap it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Then did you subsequently leave their premises?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we had coffee. I stayed for another 20 minutes and then my daughter and I left after he had left.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you meet Mira Tadic on a subsequent occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Prijedor, not with Dusko, afterwards in Trnopolje -- in Prijedor, yes, in Prijedor with Mira, yes, but not with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you go to the apartment on the next occasion in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Why did you go to the apartment on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, then I and my daughter went alone and nobody knew and there was no invitation. They had not invited me, but since they had promised to go back to Kozarac, I wanted to find out whether they had found some of our documents. So that is when we went.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you went back to the house this time, was Mira Tadic there at the time when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, when I and my daughter went to that apartment, neither Mira was there, nor Dusko's mother. There were only his two daughters there. The elder one said, "I will go and fetch my mother and grandma. They have gone to have coffee with a friend in that same building".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did Dusko Tadic's wife, Mira, and the grandma then return to the apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they did, meanwhile, 10, 15 minutes time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When they returned did you ask them about the documentation and whether they had had any luck in finding it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that was why I went, yes, I did ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What were you told?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She says, "No, there is nothing".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you at any stage say to either Mira Tadic or to Dusko Tadic that they could take possession and keep any of the documentation that was in your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, why should they keep them since when I needed them? I did not say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were in Trnopolje camp, where were you kept, where did you stay, in what part of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I and my daughter was on the upper floor of the primary school at Trnopolje. My husband was in another room, not with two of us. One of my sons was under the staircase of the school and the other one in the gymnasium.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think you briefly mentioned a moment ago that you saw Tadic, Dusko Tadic, when you were in Trnopolje camp, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you tell us the circumstances of how it is that you came to see him when you were in Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He came to look for my husband, and my younger son came to the room saying, "Ma, Dusko has arrived and there is another man with him and they are talking about something outside, outside the school".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you with your husband at this particular moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where was your husband, did you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you mean during the conversation?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No. When your son first came to you. Do you know where your husband was in the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you know, sometimes in the room where they were, since it was day time it was very stuffy, or probably in the hallway. I did not know where my husband was because I was in the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When your son came up and told you that Dusko had arrived and there was another man with him, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I ran down the stairs right away, because I was, nevertheless, afraid for him. So I went down to see that no rough words were exchanged, but I did not go near them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes. We will stand in recess for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Jakupovic, before the morning adjournment you were telling us that your son came up to you and told you that Dusko Tadic had arrived with another man and he wanted to see your husband. When you heard this you went downstairs. When you went downstairs, where did you go to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I came down from the second floor of the primary school, down the staircase into the courtyard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you went down there what did you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw my husband, Dusko Tadic and an unknown person with him, a man in a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: From where you were, were you able to hear any conversation that they had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you able to have a good view of the three of them from where you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How was Dusko Tadic dressed on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had a blue uniform with a white belt, the same pistol and a knife.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The gentleman that was with him, how was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was in a multi-coloured, a green uniform, that is, a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you stay in that spot until your husband came back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When your husband came back to you, did he say anything to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he came in scared, abnormally scared. He said, "Dusko is calling me and this man to go with them to Kozarac to sign a paper, to exchange houses with this man, this man from Velika Kladusa".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After your husband came back in, did you ever see Dusko Tadic again in the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not. I could not see. I had a daughter who was under age -- she was 12 -- and I was spending all my time with her.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Why were you spending all your time with your daughter? Was there any particular reason for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course, yes. From the guards, the military that arrived there, they were taking girls out at night. I was very afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Had you heard of this happening when you were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, very often. They were coming into the rooms at night, three or four soldiers, with flash lamps. There was no electricity. The whole time, myself and my girlfriend, we slept next to one another. There were 57 prisoners there. Every night we slept on, instead of a pillow, we would use different parts of the body of my daughter as a pillow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Why did you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To hide my child.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you hear girls being taken out of the camp when you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did you ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not girls, under age 13, 14 years, 12, whatever they would put their hands on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did you hear when they were taken out? What could you hear from where you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Myself and all my friends here, we could only cry and listen to the girls' screams. We did not hear anything but we heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did the guards do at the camp during the day? What were their duties that you were able to observe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were -- some men that were there that remained, they were taking them to a room where Kuruzovic was, Slobodan, and often they took them there, and those soldiers that were coming were under his orders probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did the guards in the camp patrol the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: There is just a little problem with the transcript that we need to fix up. When you were talking about the girls that were crying, the transcript says, "We did not hear anything but we heard". Do you mean to say that you did not see things happen but you could hear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said "seen" but, yes, we did hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You did not see but you could hear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were in the camp, what did you do in order to get food and supplies for your family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had a sister and a mother in Prijedor. My mother was old, 86. She often would bring food, flour, bread and such.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What were the conditions like in the camp where you were staying, in the part where you were staying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Where I was in that room on the top floor, there were 57 persons, an infant from three months till about the age of 80, both men and women and babies. I apologise, but for fear of going out, they would go to the bathroom in the room. They would just stay there all night.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mrs. Jakupovic, would you please now look around the courtroom and tell me if you can see the person that you know and recognise as Dule Tadic? Do you see him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you describe where he is in the courtroom and would you describe the clothes that he has on, from what you can see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dusko is between the two policemen, in a blue shirt, a multi-coloured tie and a dark blue suit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: One final question: when did you leave Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 2nd December.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mrs. Jakupovic, you asked Mira Tadic if she could find documents for you in your house. Since you had left Kozarac, you had not been back to your house, would that be right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You did not know what the state or condition was of your house after you left it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You did not know what had happened to your possessions and belongings that you had left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In relation to those documents, your husband's expired driving licence that had expired in 1985, presumably, was not an important document for you? It was not a document with which you were concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My husband never owned a car, and to me it did not mean something to look for it. What I needed were the three passports, the school certificates of the children and my personal ID. All that was in a plastic bag.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Presumably, the photographs that were brought to you by Mrs. Tadic were things of sentimental value, would that be right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you ask Mrs. Tadic or Dusko Tadic to help in relation to obtaining other papers for you that your brother may have wanted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not my brother. I did not speak of that to him at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you were in the apartment of the Tadic family in Prijedor, you told us that Dusko was just going on duty to Tukovi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is a region or an area that is near the Sana River?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There is a bridge from Prijedor that takes you across that river into Tukovi, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is all I ask.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I omitted to ask that the record reflect the identification.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, the record will reflect that the witness identified the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have no other questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Witness, where is Velika Kladusa? How far is that from Prijedor, about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Trust me, I really do not know how far it actually is.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Are you able to put a date at all on this occasion when the accused visited the camp where you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think when we arrived to Trnopolje, that was in October, I apologise, in the month of October and the date, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: About how long after you arrived was it that you saw Tadic there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, maybe 10 days into our being there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mrs. Jakupovic, do you know what is the ethnic composition of Velika Kladusa? Do you know what is the predominant religion of the people who live there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think that predominantly they are Serbs, but I would not know. I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection to Mrs. Jakupovic being permanently excused?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mrs. Jakupovic, you are permanently excused. You are free to leave. Thank you for coming.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. I call Zijad Badnjevic. ZIJAD BADNJEVIC, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sir, would you take that oath that has been handed to you, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is your full name Zijad Badnjevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 11th February 1947.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you born in Gornji Kamingrad which is in the opstina of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Gornji Kamingrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you attend primary school at Gornji Kamingrad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And secondary school in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you live in Gornji Kamingrad until 1970?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you receive training in any particular profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For a policeman of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Subsequent to your basic training, did you receive specialist training in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the nature of the specialist training you received?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was training to become an Inspector for the Criminal Technology.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When did you do your military service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From '67 till '68, '69.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you do your military service in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What is your nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your religion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Islam.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After you left Gornji Kamingrad, where did you go then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to work in the Republic Secretariat for the Interior in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Then were you subsequently transferred to the city of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was transferred in the police station. That was then called SUP Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When did this happen, when were you transferred to the SUP Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In May 1970.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you work in the SUP in Prijedor from that time in 1970 up until the commencement of the war in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, from 1970 until April 30th 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you in Prijedor when it was taken over in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Prior to the takeover of Prijedor, who was the Commander or Chief of Police in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hasan Talundzic who was electric engineer who formally worked in the iron ore mine of Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened to you in respect of your position in the police after the takeover -- in Prijedor after April 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 30th April, I went to work as usual. At 6.30 I left my house. In front of the building of the police station I was met by Kovacevic Ranko, Petrovic Radoslav, and another soldier and there was a fourth one. They demanded that I should raise hands, that they will -- that we, as Croats and Muslims, could no longer go on working in this building until our fate is determined.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you taken to the SUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they searched -- they did a body search, and then they ordered that I follow them into the SUP building, and they took me to room 2 which was part of the security of the SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After some time were you subsequently taken into the new head of police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was Simo Drljaca, who before that worked in the cultural and educational organisation, who was from Sanski Most where I was born too. I knew him slightly and he did not know me at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you went to see him, what did he say to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Cadjo Milutin was sitting with him. He introduced him. At that time he was a retired policeman and he was activated and he took over a separate police station of the reserves who did the most harm to our people, and he introduced me to Simo Drljaca with a name and last name, and he introduced him to me, where Simo offered me to sign a statement of a paper, A4, written in Cyrillic alphabet, to sign and to join in their service. If I did not sign that, myself and other Bosniaks and Croats will not be able to be present or work in this Secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you recall the nature of the document, what it said in approximate terms? I do not expect you to remember it word for word, but what was the general thrust of the document that you signed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The document was, as I said, written in Cyrillic alphabet. The memo said: "Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbian Ministry of Interior.
