This station of Prijedor", and I do not know the exact number, and date and down there in block letters it was a solemn declaration and then myself and then blank for the name, "I solemnly declare that as a member of the security forces of the Serb Republic will respect and protect the interests of the Serb Republic, and the interests of the citizens", and in the end what was conspicuous to me, "in case it would be needed, I also give my life to the Serb state" and then it was "Prijedor" and the date left, and then it was a space left for signature. That was approximately the contents of this solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you sign this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. I offered to Simo Drljaca and Milutin Cadjo to give me a deadline, a reasonable one, of a week so that I could talk to my colleagues, with my colleagues Bosnians and Croats, to address my Ministry, at that time the Ministry of the Interior in Sarajevo, to talk to my family, to my friends, my colleagues. If we all agreed, I will also go, but if we did not, I am not going to sign off on the loyalty myself. They gave us a reasonable seven day deadline and told us to call, if we did not agree, "you should leave the Secretariat and you should not be present in this building any more".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you ever sign this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. That document remained with me in the pocket. I went back to the -- to my office. I left it in my desk. I am sorry that I did not have a chance to take this document, but I had no option.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened after that, after you had refused to sign to your future with the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That all of us who refused, we had a meeting. There was a Minister from the Ministry in Banja Luka, that all the Bosniaks and Croats who were there, professionals, and all Serbs who were working there were present at this meeting in the iron ore mine of Ljubija. We refused to sign because that system, that state, was not the one that we expected and, collectively, we refused to sign this loyalty document. After that, what followed were individual arrests and taking into the camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you arrested and taken to a camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on 3rd June 1992, in early morning hours, I was arrested. I was taken to the Omarska camp, then to Trnopolje and in the end I got out of Prijedor and my country.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How long were you in the camp at Omarska for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From June 3rd, late evening hours, until 7th August 1992. Then I was transferred to the Trnopolje camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were in Omarska camp, were you there with any of your relatives or fellow policemen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We were mixed. There was my brother, Nijaz Badnjevic; my uncle, Velid Badnjevic, who was killed me and Nijaz was taken on July 27th, and we do not know about him since; Sadikovic Ago, who was taken away on June 25th -- July 25th; Mirzad Alisic, Sinanagic Emir, Fazlic Muhamed and my other colleagues and friends and neighbours, Muslims, Bosniaks and Croats. We were all mixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In total, how many friends and relatives of yours either died or disappeared in Omarska camp that you have not seen since?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of my 35 colleagues, policemen, who worked in different duties in the police force, from that time of the camps and had disappeared, for some I could affirm that they were killed and others were taken from the prison and others, my neighbours' friends. There is a huge list I can give, I do not know it by heart, but I can give you some names. Those were people who lay down with me, who suffered with me, and I affirm that they were taken from our rooms and they were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During the time that you were in Omarska camp, were you ever beaten or otherwise mistreated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, everybody went through some form of torture in that camp and I, like my other neighbours and colleagues, I also went through beatings during the lunch time, that one sole meal, and then while going to use the toilet and any other moment, they were beating us, abused us, provoked, and did with us what nobody could -- what no man could do to another man. They had prerogatives that nobody could give to anybody. An animal would not do to another animal what they did to us, other people, to us as people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know the accused in these proceedings, Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When did you first meet him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I met Dusko Tadic when I was on official duty. I did not know him privately until then. After that I knew him both privately and officially.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When was it that you first knew him, first met him, I should say? Approximately, the year will be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In around '89, mid '89, that is when I was engaged in Criminal Investigation Technology and in the police station at Kozarac, and there Dusan Tadic had reported the rape of his brother's daughters, or one of his brother's daughters. He was, I believe, from Banja Luka. Then I made part of the team engaged to investigate this grave offence which is rape which he had reported to the police station, and the police station was subordinate to the centre in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say the police station, that is the Kozarac police station was subordinate to the Prijedor police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did the complaint specify who it was that was alleged to have perpetrated this rape?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Dusan Tadic was found in the police station at Kozarac together with a girl who was about 15 or 16 years of age in tears, frightened. The policeman on duty informed us that this was a gentleman who had reported the rape of his brother's daughter, and that the rape had been perpetrated by boys of her age, young men, Muslims, in Kozarac right next to the police station and roughly across the street which is about seven metres wide next to the pavement, that it had been done by young men, that he had entered around 3 o'clock in the morning into that house -- I believe the house was owned by Suljo -- and that he beat and battered them and threw them down the stairs and took out that girl, his brother's daughter, to the police station and reported the rape in order to substantiate the claims of the alleged Muslim threat to Serbs because the Serbs were a minority in that part of Kozarac, about two or three per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was the girl, the victim of the rape, subsequently examined professionally by a gynaecologist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What were the results of that examination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The gynaecological examination was performed by the doctor on duty at the hospital at the gynaecological department in Prijedor, Ziko Canic. He is in [redacted] at present, a refugee like me. He, therefore, examined the girl. In his finding it was said that there were no signs of violence on the girl or any sexual intercourse.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was the girl then subsequently interviewed by police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Together with me, the team included Gostimir Modic, a Serb from Prijedor, together with me -- he came from Celinac -- we were both hired at the same time, we were together on the team. In an interview with the girl which he conducted but separate from his uncle, that he had invented it all and reported falsely because she had agreed it with the neighbours because she liked to come to Kozarac, to see her friends and socialise with them, and they had agreed that that night they should make a party, a dance in that house, to sit and drink and sing and to spend the night like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So she admitted that she was, in fact, not raped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, she told us that it was no go, that "my uncle had invented it and ordered me to tell that, I was forced by him to say that, and I tell you openly that nothing of that sort happened". Through our operative work and our attempts to talk to those boys, they were children, and other neighbours, that nothing had happened, that the rape had not happened and we found that it was a false report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You said just in your answer there that she said her "uncle" had invented it, by the word "uncle" do you mean Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that was Dusko Tadic and I always referred to Dusko Tadic, because he met us at the police station in Kozarac and told us that his niece had been raped and that we were to undertake our official duties to find, identify, the culprits and detain them and all the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Later in 1990, you were assigned to conduct another investigation in relation to some letters that had been received allegedly by the accused Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you tell us the circumstances of how it is that you became involved in that investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was sometime in the latter half of '89 and in '90, Dusan Tadic from Kozarac reported directly to the Prijedor police station with my then head, Ranko Mijic, that he had received an anonymous letter from an unknown person of a threatening nature, one, and the second and only when he received the third one, we, that is, our office, was compelled at his intervention to seriously undertake the investigation of the criminal offence of anonymous letter writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the nature of the letters were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The letter was of a threatening content. It was handwritten on the paper form A4 and its contents, I can tell you roughly. "You", and it was addressed to Dusan Tadic, Kozarac, I do not remember the street, whether it was Mladena Stojanovica or Marsala Tita Street, I cannot remember now, "You, the Serbs from Kozarac, you have to move out. You go to Serbia. This is Bosnia. This will be Turkey and we shall live here". This was more or less the contents of the third letter, and it ended in a message, "We shall wage jihad", "jihad" the holy war, "We shall exterminate you", and it ended in a message, we thought it was a message, but it was nothing in Arabic, written in Arabic, an Arabic text which I and my other colleagues did not manage to interpret or read because we did not know Arabic. So we turned to effendi from Kozarac. He was a religious worker. His name was Ilijaz Mahmuljin from Kozarac. He worked as effendi in the central Kozarac mosque and he read and interpreted to us the contents of that Arabic text.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did you discover it meant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With me in company was Inspector Mirsad Alisic who, as of July '92, is gone. He was with me, together with me, in Omarska. We turned to Mr. Ilijaz, effendi from Kozarac, to interpret it. We were in his house. We sat down and he gave us the finding that that was nothing, that there was an Arabic letter here and there, but that the contents could not be read, that the writer of that letter had tried to rewrite, to transcribe, it from somewhere but that it had no meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you then subject these letters to any further investigation in order to determine who it may have been that wrote the letter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, since I was directly responsible for that kind of work, we decided to work together operatively and to use various CI technology and criminal evidence, which we did. We took the handwriting samples of those persons who were indicated by us to Dusan Tadic -- by Dusan Tadic as possible authors of the letter. So that I took the handwriting sample from three young men in Kozarac following all the criminal investigation rules. I did that at the police station in Prijedor, and also the sample of Dusan Tadic. By comparing this and with former samples, as required by the Criminal Investigation Technology, I sent it to the expert service in Sarajevo to the CID department division for Criminal Investigation Technology.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you subsequently receive a report back relating to this handwriting analysis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we received a finding sometime in 1990. I can remember it more or less. The expert could not say who was the author of the letter, but he said that the author of the letter had tried to avoid his personal handwriting, that he tried to forge it so that the expert analysis could not establish who had written it, and through operative work we were more or less on the way of finding out who had written that letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The three men that Dusko Tadic had indicated who may have been the perpetrators, were they found not to be, was there handwriting not the same handwriting as that contained in the letter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all the suspects who were on the list then, which included also his sister-in-law, that is one of his brother's sisters called Zlata, a Muslim from Kozarac, her maiden name was Ziska. My colleague, Reuf Travancic, took a sample of her handwriting, and the finding was that of the suspects who were on the list and Mrs. Zlata's handwriting, that it was not theirs, that is that the letter had not been written by them. We received such confirmation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So what then happened to the investigation after these findings? What did you then do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We continued with our operative work, with field work. We spoke to neighbours, to witnesses and other people whom he had put on the list and who might be possibly considered as alleged letter writers. I can give you only one name, because other people I know, other people I do know but I cannot give you their names for justified reasons because these people are missing, they disappeared from my company in Omarska where I was also in the camp, and they are entered as missing. They are on records as missing people, and if I mention their names here it might be a mistake because something might befall these people. But I personally think that these people are still alive and, therefore, I can give their particulars to the Court subsequently. I can give you only the name of one person who is also a refugee.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We do not have to go into that. Going back to during the course of the war, did you then go to Trnopolje camp on 7th August 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on 7th August together with about 750 inmates from Omarska I was transferred by buses to Keraterm, sorry, to Trnopolje and arrived there around 2300 hours at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have been told there is a word that needs redaction at 12.33.06 on page 44 line 4. I apply to have that redacted, just the name of the place, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Badnjevic, when you arrived at Trnopolje camp can you tell us the conditions of the camp when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I arrived on the last bus. I told you around 2300 there was no electricity. That whole area perhaps was without electricity. So they drove us into the camp which at that time had a wire fence around it. In front of the camp there was a throng of women, children, old people, emaciated, young and there were guards at the gate. We were driven inside and we were ordered to sit down wherever we happened to be and to wait for the next day because one could not go inside as they were full. That is what we did and we waited for the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you just tell us what was the camp composed of? What buildings was it composed of when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The camp used the old building, the once cultural centre called, and the surgery, the ambulanta on the ground floor. Upstairs there was a small room where there were also inmates left. Over the gate there was an older building which once was a purchasing station and a buildings material store, and above that part of that cultural centre a new primary school had been built. It was also full and the yard was full of tanks covered with plastic and blankets, because people had made some makeshift accommodation and lived there in the mud, in the dust.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know where the Commander of the camp lived, sorry, where the Commander of the camp's office was when you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Across the cultural centre there was a private house which once used to house a restaurant. Its owners changed. I cannot remember the name of the last owner. In one wing the then Red Cross, the local Red Cross, was accommodated and in another room the Commander was somewhere there. I did not go there. I did not enter those rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were in Trnopolje camp were you beaten or otherwise mistreated by any of the guards at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As usual and also all the others all the time as we waited for water or for lunch a guard would come by and kick one with a foot, with the baton, with a hand. I did not spend much time in that camp. I was released from there on the basis of a medical finding, of the doctor's findings as I was severely mentally ill.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When were you released, can you remember, from Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 13th August I was allowed to go home to my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That was back to Prijedor, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, to Prijedor to my flat where I used to live before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you go back there until November 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, together with my family I spent, I went through the same predicament similar to the Omarska camp, because my freedom of movement was limited, the quantity of food was also limited, and everything else that a normal man could experience. I could only watch from the balcony. My freedom of movement was restricted. I was not allowed to go out of the apartment or from the building because it was an apartment building, there were 120 flats in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you in November 1992 go in a convoy to Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you, please, now look around the courtroom and tell me if you recognise the person that you know as Dule Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Could you point to that person. Would you describe where he is in the courtroom and how he is dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is sitting between two policemen facing one another. He has a tie, a light blue shirt, a dark blue suit. Anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No. Might the record reflect, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, the record will reflect that the witness identified the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Badnjevic, you knew Mr. Tadic as Dusan Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dusan Tadic I believe that is his first name and surname and Dusko was his pet name. So whether he is Dusan or Dusko it is of no relevance to me. I know that it is the man whom I saw, Dusan or Dusko Tadic from Kozarac, a Serb who for a while was an active athlete, who was an inhabitant of Kozarac, with a wife, with two children. If that is not that man let him say so. If he is, let him also say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I was not suggesting to you that it was not the man that you knew, but that you knew him not as Dule Tadic, you knew him as Dusan Tadic which is how you referred to him in court, is that not right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as Dusan Tadic. I think that is his name Dusan and he was also called Dule, and that is what I know about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you asked by any of the other brothers of Dusan Tadic questions about the condition of the niece whom it was alleged to have been raped by the young men at the party in the house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you repeat it, please? I missed the beginning of your question. Which one of Dusan's brothers do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I was asking you whether any of the brothers, rather than any particular one that I could name to you, but any of the other members of the family also spoke to you about their concerns with the young girl who had been in the house at the party until 3 o'clock in the morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, nobody enquired from Dusan Tadic's.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You did not speak to Mladen Tadic, for instance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You did not speak to the father of the girl?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I thought you investigated this matter. You did not enquire about the family of the girl as to her circumstances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She came to visit, to pay a visit of her uncle and her parents thought that she was being looked after in the house, because at that time he could be her parent or a guardian, a protector.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So it seems Mr. Tadic was very concerned about her welfare and where she had been, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I guess so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: After the various examinations and the findings made by the police, that was the end of the matter in relation to these allegations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, the file was completed, the case was completed. It was also submitted to the Public Prosecutor, the Investigating Magistrate and together with my then boss, Ranko Mijic, took the decision on it because I and my colleagues could not, of course, decide what would happen to the case, but the Public Prosecutor and Investigating Magistrate could. I presume they shelved that case judging, presumably, that there was no need to work on it any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So, as far as you know, that was the end of the matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I have nothing further to ask.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Witness, you formed the opinion that this was a false report made by Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We established through operative work, interviews with those boys and girls, there were about 15 of them in that house, that everything was quite normal in that house.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Yes. I am just concerned with your conclusion. Did you charge Mr. Tadic with making a false report to the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The conclusion was that the report was false and we did not succeed to charge for the false report, because my jurisdiction and my colleagues' jurisdiction did not extend over this. All of this was in the Public Prosecutor's and the Investigating Magistrates' office. They had the case in their hands so they could do that.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Nothing more happened after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, nothing because somebody must have ordered to shelve the whole case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Nothing, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to Mr. Badnjevic being permanently excused?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sir, you are permanently excused. That means you are free to leave. Thank you very much for coming. We will stand in recess until 2.30 for lunch.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: (2.30 p.m.) PRIVATE

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Miss Hollis, will you call the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, the Prosecution calls Mustafa Mujkanovic. MR. MUSTAFA MUJKANOVIC, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sir, would you please take the oath that is being handed to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, would you please state your name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mustafa Mujkanovic.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 24th July 1947.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What is your nationality or ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was your place of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was that in the village itself or in a hamlet near the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A hamlet.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you attend primary school in Trnopolje for four years and then for four years in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you leave school at age 15?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you then work as a baker's apprentice in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: After that did you go to Slovenia to train as a bricklayer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you then work as a bricklayer in Slovenia for some 13 years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: During that time how often did you visit Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Almost every weekend.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: While you were living in Slovenia were you called to do your compulsory military service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you serve in the JNA for 15 months starting in 1969?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What were your duty in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a border guard.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where did you perform those duties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in training at Klana near Rijeka, and then after the training I went to Ohrid, to the Albanian border, and when there was aggression on Czechoslovakia, as we called it, then I went to Dimitrovgrad near Pirot, to the Bulgarian border.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Dimitrovgrad was in what Republic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: During your service with the JNA, did you become familiar with JNA uniforms, insignia, weapons, vehicles and equipment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: After working in Slovenia for some 13 years, did you then return to Trnopolje and open your own business?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What kind of business was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in construction, an object from the foundation to the keys.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What local areas did you work in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Bosanski Novi, Prijedor, Banja Luka, Kozarac, Laktasi and many other places.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How often did you work in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Every now and then. Sometimes I would work three months in a row and sometimes maybe a month. It depended on business.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What types of construction did you do in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did mostly houses, some other structures like kebab houses and such.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you do similar construction projects in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: In addition to your work in the local areas, did you work outside the local areas as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where did you work outside the local area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I worked in Slovenia, Croatia, Serbia, I worked around Bosnia, and the last three or four years, I do not know precisely, I worked in Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you were working outside the local area, how long would you be gone at a time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometimes a month I was away from home, sometimes two. It could be three months, but that was rarely. When I come back home, I stay home 10, 15, 20 days, depending on the business.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you were not travelling, how often would you visit Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not daily, but in eight days two or three times, sometimes more, sometimes daily.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: In addition to the work that you did in Kozarac, what other reasons would take you to Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had friends.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: In December 1991, did you return to Trnopolje and remain there until you were taken to Trnopolje detention camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: If the witness could be provided with Prosecution Exhibit 305, please? Sir, I would like you to take a look at this map which is an enlarged map of an area of Trnopolje. If you could locate your house on the map and then I will ask that the map be put on the overhead projector, please? Sir, looking at this map, if you could point to your home as it appears on this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (The witness indicated on the map).

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So it is a house that is to the right of the yellow road marked on the map? It is the second road to the right as you go up from the school, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: It is just beyond the intersection of that second road to the right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, had you lived in that location your entire life when you lived in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you know Dule Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How long have you known him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Many, many years.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew him while I was still in Kozarac, I was at Versad Kulasic as an apprentice. It is on the same side as you go to the Mount Kozara from the road Banja Luka/Prijedor, it is on the right-hand side, and the distance between the bakery and the house of Dusan's father was the distance of 40 to 50 metres at the most and Dusan, as a child, he was small, was coming for our fresh baked goods. That is how -- that is from when I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Is Dusko Tadic younger or older than you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Younger.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you know any other members of his family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who did you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew his brother, Ljubo. I knew the other two brothers from sight, but one of them was, I cannot remember his name, but Ljubo I knew and mother and father I knew.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you know his wife?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From sight, I know she worked in Kozarac at the hospital, and I know that she is from a place near Kozarac called Vidovici, that she was born there.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: During the time that you knew Dusko Tadic, what kind of contact did you have with him other than when he would visit the bakery at which you worked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He came to the bakery for a couple of years and then I saw him as he was growing up and as I was, and I would see him often times.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When he became an adult, did you continue to have contact with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no direct contact. I did not associate with him, but just in passing. We greet, you raise your hand. That is the way I would meet him. Often times, I would be sitting in a cafe or in some coffee bar with music. I saw him in Prijedor often times, often times in Banja Luka. I do not know how long back, I cannot recall, but his brothers had a club, a karate club, in Banja Luka. So I saw him in Banja Luka. I saw him. He had a friend who was a neighbour of mine, Radivoje Milutinovic, so occasionally I would see him with him, and so .....

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you were not travelling, on an average, how many times a month do you think you would see Dule Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depended. If you take a season, let us say, I worked in Kozarac and I did a kebab house, that was 30 metres away across from Dule's house, so then I would see him four or five times. But there would be times when I would not see him for two months. If you take a season, I would see him often times, but I did not pay attention. We did not pay attention how many times you meet a person. I had no -- I did not keep, have any registration of that.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkanovic, do you know what businesses Dule Tadic was involved in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Karate for a time and then lately -- but do not take my word for it -- I think around 1990 he opened a cafe.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you ever go to that cafe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not go to cafes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you know where that cafe was located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where was it located in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the old road, from the intersection when you go towards Kozarac on the right-hand side, at the very corner as you turn towards the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you know what businesses were located across the street from the cafe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What businesses were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Directly across, there was a house and then there was a building, an apartment building, and then there was another one with apartments upstairs, and downstairs, if we go from Mount Kozara to the right, was a barber shop. Next to the barber shop was a pharmacy. Next to the pharmacy was for a while a book store, and then I do not know what, it was also a store but I cannot tell you what.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: During the time that you knew Dule Tadic as an adult, did you ever see him with a beard or facial hair?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew Dule when he was not, he did not grow a beard, and then I would see him with or without beard.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: After the Serb takeover of Prijedor on 30th April, did you ever travel to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you travelled to Prijedor, did you see soldiers in the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you ever hear any of these soldiers speaking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you hear any dialects that were not local?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What dialects did you hear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serbian and Montenegrin.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Before the attack on Kozarac, did the inhabitants of Trnopolje village receive any ultimatums?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What were those ultimatums?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To turn in the weapons and that people would be detained who were, I do not know how they called them, extremes, that they would be interrogated, and who was guilty was going to be going to Banja Luka and who was not guilty would be sent back home.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you have any weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When the town of Kozarac was shelled, was any area of Trnopolje shelled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but not with the force as Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: After the attack on Kozarac, did any refugees come to the village of Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did any of these refugees come to your home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, those who lived across the asphalt up there.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: From what villages did the refugees come to your home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kamicani, Mujici, Brdjani, Besici, I mean Kozarusa. I mean, families that I had and my wife had.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was the ethnic group of the refugees who came to your home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was the nationality or ethnic group of the refugees who came to your home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How close was your home to the Trnopolje detention camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think about 700 metres.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When did you first see any detainees in the camp at Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall exactly, 26th or 27th May '92.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: After these detainees were brought to the camp at Trnopolje, did women from the town of Trnopolje take food to the detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, for a while.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When did the cleansing of your area occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my area, the cleansing came on 9th June '92.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What area was cleansed on that date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly this vicinity of the camp.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where were you on 9th June when this cleansing occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At home.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How many other people were at home with you on that date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you think altogether, including women, children, men, elderly, about 35 to 40 of us.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: On that date where were you and the other people in your home taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were taken in the direction of the camp, and men were separated in the camp and women and children to the railroad station, railway station, and they put them on the train in the direction of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you were taken to Trnopolje camp, did you recognise any of the men who took you there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I recognised.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The ones that you recognised where were they from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly, they were local people of Serbian nationality.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Multi-colour -- when I say multi-colour it is the camouflage uniform -- and SMB clothes, that was SMB, but that was the winter uniform. It was not kamgarn. That was a rolled wool. Kamgarn is worn by the officers.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you say SMB uniforms, you mean the uniforms of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: These are the uniforms that are an olive green in colour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How long were you held at the Trnopolje detention camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until 1st October '92.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: While you were held in the camp, where were you held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: School building.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where were you held in the school building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the top floor, in the toilet.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What could you see from that toilet room that you were held in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could see the west side, that is, towards Prijedor. There was a road that leads Trnopolje to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: While you were at the camp, were you allowed to go outside the school building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For a while, no, and then later, yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you were allowed to go outside the school building, where were you allowed to go within the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly within the perimeter.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you first arrived at Trnopolje camp, where was the Serbian Red Cross office located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In a building, in the front off the road on the lower floor.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What building was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dom, it is not the school, it is the dom.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Is that a hall with a cinema?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but on the front part next to the road.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did that Serbian Red Cross office move to another location while you were at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where was it moved to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Moved across the street, across the road, in a restaurant, I do not know exactly when, but in any event before the women were to arrive from Omarska, two weeks before that.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: If at this time we could have Prosecution Exhibit 203 played, that is, the video of Trnopolje camp? Sir, I am going to ask you to look at the screen in front of you while we show a video. If we could stop the video here, please? Sir, is this the school building in which you were kept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: If we could move forward, please? If we could stop here? Sir, what is this building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A shop.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall what offices were in the portion of that building, that is, behind it, behind the shop?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was behind that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the right and on the upper floor in the back, there was the storage space for the shop, that is, the supplies, the stock. To the left above, that is out here, was the centre and there was the door where doctors were, the blood laboratory, Local Commune, and a restaurant called Moco and that is where the Red Cross was. So in the back, not here, here was only the shop.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Could we go forward, please? Will you stop here? Sir, if you see this building, the large white building with the arches, what building is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That is where the restaurant was first and then the Red Cross. On the upper floor at that time were the headquarters on the upper floor.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: If we look at this picture now, we see a small rectangular building to the left. It appears to have three doors. What is that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are three brick toilets.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: If we could move forward, please? If we could stop there? What is this building that we see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was the warehouse for building materials, where they kept the stock of them.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: If we could move forward? As we turn this corner on to this road to our right, in what direction are we heading?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Towards Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Is this also the road that went in the direction of Elezovici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean to Elezovici.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: In the direction, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Then if we could fast forward it to the next clip, please? If we could play it beginning with the buildings across from the camp? Will you stop here? What is this building that we see on the right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the building where the Red Cross was and part of the headquarters, although the main command was in another place. That is across the centre. I have already told you about it.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: If we could move forward, please? As we are looking at these houses here, do you know the ethnic group of the people who owned these houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: While you were at the camp, were these houses that are being shown here being used by camp personnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The houses that we saw to the right, while you were at the camp in Trnopolje, were those houses being used by camp personnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The camp personnel, yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could shut off that tape, please? Did you know any of the other detainees at Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, many.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was the ethnic group of the detainees that you knew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslims, Catholics, Romany.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you know the Camp Commander prior to your coming to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who was the Camp Commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kuruzovic, Slobodan.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How had you known him before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, not really closely, by sight.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you know what his ethnic group was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Serb.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What would he wear when he was in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, logically, he wore a camouflage uniform all the time.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you ever see any rank insignia on that uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What rank insignia did you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As of a Major.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you know any of the guards that worked at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, several.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The ones that you knew, where were they from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were mostly locals.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you know any people named Karajica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I knew several Karajicas.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did any of those people work at the camp while you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the first names of the Karajicas who worked at Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of some of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Please tell us the names that you recall.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sreto Karajica were there, Mladen worked there, and now I cannot remember all of them, but they worked there, a number of them worked there.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How were Sreto and Mladen related?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Father and son.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who was the father?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sreto was.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: At this time if we could play Prosecution Exhibit 307 for identification? It is a video tape. Sir, we are looking at an area -- if we could stop here, please -- near Trnopolje. Do you recognise any of those homes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who lived in those homes that are shown on this video tape here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This one here was the home of Sveto Karajica and his younger son, and Sreto's house is below this one.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So Sveto was related to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sveto or Svetozar. He would respond to both those names.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, how was Sveto related to Sreto?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sveto was Sreto's father.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: If we could move forward, please? If we could stop here, please? Sir, do you recognise whose house this is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who owned this house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember his name, but I know it was Bajro Cuskic's son who worked in Switzerland. That was his property. But when we were driven to the camp, Sreto Karajica's son moved into this house.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall which son that was who moved into the house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The elder.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have just mentioned it.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Stariji is his name? Sir, what was the name of the older son who moved into this house, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mladen.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: That was the Mladen who worked at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: All right, thank you. If we could shut that video off, please? Did you know a family named Cavic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did any of those family members work at the camp or visit the camp often?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of any of the Cavic family who worked at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What are the names that you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Milan and Dragoje or, rather, Mile.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Both of them worked at Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mile was guard Commander for a while.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you know what Dragoje's position was at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dragoje, as they called him, was a field man, so he was not at the guard point but he was always present in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When he came to the camp would he mistreat detainees there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you know a family named Nisevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nisevic maybe.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Nisevic. Did any of those family members work at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of any of those family members who worked at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Something.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was Goran Nisevic called Cigo. Some others also worked there but I cannot remember their names now.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you know a family named Baltic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Baltic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did any members of that family work at Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, some of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of any of the Baltic family that worked in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I only know them by sight.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, while you were in Trnopolje camp, were you ever beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Several times.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were there any times that were particularly severe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Twice, yes, rather severe.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: These two beatings that were rather severe, where did they occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in the building next to the centre called "Laboratory". It was the blood laboratory. That was at the entrance. As you go to see the doctor, to the left there was a door and it says "Laboratory".

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, the first time you were taken there and beaten, did you recognise who took you there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mladen Mitrovic.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How did you know him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew him for a long time before that he married a girl from my place. He lives in Prijedor otherwise, but he worked as a waiter in my locality for quite sometime so that I knew him. On a winter day when there would be no bus or train, I frequently gave him a lift home.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was his ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mixed. His mother is a Ukrainian and father a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How often would he come to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was always in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did he work there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When he worked at the camp what did he wear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: When you were taken to the lab and beaten, did you recognise any of the people who took part in that beating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, one Slavko from Prijedor, a Captain by rank -- I mean, I saw the insignia, three stars, that is a captain -- and he interrogated me. I do not know, he was a butcher in Prijedor. I believe his family name was "Puhovski" or something like that, and those others, I saw they had uniforms but I knew where I was, and I did not really bother about recognising anyone. It would have been of no use to me whether I knew anyone or not.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, the uniforms that these men wore, did the uniforms have any kind of insignia on them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, there were, there were. There were kokardas also on their caps or on those caps. There are round caps and there are former military caps, the ones that the former Yugoslav Army used to wear.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You say that they had kokardas on their caps, can you tell us what a kokarda is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you want me to explain what a kokarda is, what it signifies or both?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Both, please. What is a kokarda?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kokarda is a Chetnik symbol, a wartime Chetnik symbol. It is from World War II. It was then the sign of Drazen Mihajlovic. It is a two-headed eagle, and those kokardas are worn in war. Drazen Mihajlovic used them in World War II and it was used now. What does it signify? It is the same, or I guess so, it is the same as when a Croat -- I do not want to offend anyone, but when a Croat puts, if a Croat puts a letter "U" on his flag rather than the chessboard, or a German, if a German put a swastika cross on the flag, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The people that were in the room, this first time that you were beaten, did any of the people in that room use a non-local dialect when they spoke?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was the dialect or accent that you recognised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From Serbia and Montenegro, they were people who came up from outside most probably.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: During this first beating that you received, what was used to beat you with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They beat me with anything, from baseball bat to cables, to boots, hands and even a chair.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did they appear to concentrate the blows on any parts of your body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where did they concentrate those blows?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the area of my heart and kidneys, but otherwise all over the body. They beat all over, including my head.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What injuries or bruising did you receive as a result of this beating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first time one of my veins in my leg is cut, my head was fractured -- it was broken here. There were fractures here, like this, five or six centimetres, and I had many such injuries. The second time, if you are asking me about the second time?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you about the second incident itself. The second beating that occurred, how long after the first beating did it occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had just begun to recover. I cannot remember, perhaps four or five days after it I was taken in once again.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you recognise who took you for the second beating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, it was the same man, so to speak, that Mladen, but there were others too who were in his company. Cigo was there. I mean, he is our neighbour and around there, but they mostly laughed. Some were in front of me, some were at my back and they laughed, but there were a number of them to the door. Then they opened the door and I entered and then, well, and then I knew what was in store.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You said that Mladen was one who took you there, what is Mladen's last name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mitrovic.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You said Cigo, what is Cigo's last name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Goran Nisevic.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The second occasion that you were beaten, what did they use to beat you with on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Anything, rifle butt. I had four teeth struck out on the right-hand side. Two were also kicked out on the left one, and this here, here as you see on the ----

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What happened ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: --- below my eyes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: --- to your eyes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was, it was bruised, it was bruised because there was blood had coagulated and then a friend, a doctor, helped me who was not supposed to but he did, he risked, and he gave me some medicines and so I still feel the effects.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you lose consciousness either time you were beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they beat me and beat me. I do not even remember how long. It looked like eternity to me. Eventually, one took me by my feet and put me against the wall and the other one began to beat me with his hands, with his feet, so that I felt sick, I threw up. Then suddenly I wanted to throw up again but I could not, and there was some yellow liquid which I vomited. It was so bitter that I have never tasted in my life anything so bitter and then I must have fainted.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you ever told why you were being beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, several times, yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Why were they beating you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were asking for rifle, for money, for gold.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: While you were in the Trnopolje camp, do you recall an occasion when you saw a column of people coming toward the camp from the direction of Elezovici and that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you able to recognise any of the people in that group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I could not recognise them.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where were you when you saw this group coming toward the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in the WC on the upper floor, this is, as I told you, a view towards Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The next day after seeing this column, do you recall being called out to bury bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the following day. It was 10th July when I buried bodies, and on the 9th they were brought in and killed.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who called you out to bury these bodies on 10th July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Goran Nisevic. He was the guard Commander at the time.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where were you taken to bury these bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the direction of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of the corpses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who did you recognise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recognised Meula Idrizvic, her son, Sadik, their daughter-in-law I recognised, Munib Hodzic I recognised. I recognised a young one, there was a lad, I believe his name was Samir Elezovic. I recognised a couple of them more, but I am not quite sure because some had half of their head missing, or the whole head would be covered in blood, so that -- but altogether about 13 persons buried.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: That first name, is that a woman's name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, she is a woman close on to 70 at the time.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was her first name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Meula Redzic.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The people that you recognised, the bodies that you recognised, what was their ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Was there a mill that was located close to Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the direction of Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you ever taken to that mill to bury bodies there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who took you to the mill to bury bodies there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once it was Dragoje Cavic to bury Ante Mrgolja and his son. I know Ante Mrgolja well and his son as well. I am not sure whether his name was Goran or Zoran, one of the two it is.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You mean the son's name is either Goran or Zoran?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: You said that Dragoje Cavic took you there, and you saw the bodies ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: --- of Ante Mrgolja and his son. What was the ethnic group of Ante Mrgolja and his son?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Catholic.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you see any wounds or injuries on these bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What did you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was, I saw that they had six, the wires, that was, that is the wire that is used in construction as armature, it is six millimetres cross-section, and I saw that two wires that were pierced through their tongues, and I saw on their necks, but I could not see what. I was afraid to look more closely, whether they had firearms wounds or some other objects, but in any event they were dead.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So you saw wounds on their necks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Were you taken to this mill on other occasions to bury people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you recognise any other people that you had to bury there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I recognised them.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who did you recognise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The second time I recognised the Foric’s. There were two brothers, two brothers and two brothers, a total of six and, as we called it, there were three sets of brothers from three brothers.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: On this occasion who took you there to bury these bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dragoje took me, Cavic.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you recognise any wounds or injuries on these bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were killed by firearms, point blank.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: What was the ethnic group of these Foric brothers whose bodies you buried?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: At this time if we could continue with Prosecution Exhibit 307 for identification?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Miss Hollis, do you recall the Exhibit that we had and we were to refer to persons by either their letter or number?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is not implicated at this time, is it?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: No, it is not.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Can we play the second part of that video, please? If we could stop? Back up just a bit, please? Just come up to where we can see this road to the right, please? Stop here. Sir, do you recognise where this road to the right leads?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where does that road lead?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That road leads, it leads from Trnopolje towards Omarska. This road that goes to the left is the road to Cavici, and if you are coming from the direction of Omarska, it is the road to the right is the one to Cavici.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: So, as we are looking at this now, the road that leads to the right is the road to Cavici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: On that road to Cavici, is there any type of cemetery near that road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there is. From this asphalt, 150 metres, I do not think there is more, maybe not even that much, to the left there is a cemetery, Orthodox.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: If we could go forward, please? As we are going back into Trnopolje on this road, if you could tell us when we approach the mill, please? Is that the mill that we just passed? If we could stop, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Back it up, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that is not it. We just passed by it.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, can we stop here, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That, yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Is this the mill where you were taken to bury the bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: If we could go forward? Right, thank you very much. Your Honour, at this time I would offer Prosecution Exhibit 307 for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 307 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Mr. Mujkanovic, do you recall an occasion when you were taken to bury bodies near your home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who took you to bury these bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Miso Radulovic and another man. I know him by sight. I know that he was in the municipality working as a driver. I do not know his name.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of these bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Who did you recognise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recognised some, Tefa, I knew him by sight, I know he was from Kamicani and that he worked in Germany for a long time, and Meho Krajina. Tefa was cut by rifles and then Meho had his throat slashed, and then 20 to 30 metres from there I found my brother, my oldest brother. He was stabbed five times in the chest by either a knife or a bayonet, left breast was cut off. I apologise, but I have to say his genitals were cut off and he was also slashed over his throat.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, what was your oldest brother's name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Esef.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: While you were at the camp, did you ever see women or girls taken from the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did see.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: How many times did you yourself see this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw it twice.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: The first time that you saw it where were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first time I was between the home (sic) and those brick latrines that you were showing earlier.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Sir, the translation says you were between the "home" and the brick latrines, did you say the "dom"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Where were these women or girls being brought from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ones were behind the dom, there were tents there, and the others were taken out of the hall, the dom.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: In what direction were these women or girls being taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were taken in the direction of the road, that is, towards the Red Cross in the direction of the road.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Without naming them, did you recognise any of these women or girls who were being taken away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I was not given permission to mention their names.
